lesson.title: Not the Same Thing: Untangling Heat from Temperature
lesson.summary: Heat is energy transferred between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference, while temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of a substance's particles, and mixing the two up leads to real errors in predicting what will happen.
lesson.body:
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, atoms, molecules, or ions, that make up a substance: how fast, on average, those particles are moving, vibrating, or jiggling. Heat is something different. Heat is energy that is transferred, or flowing, from a warmer region or object to a cooler one as a direct result of that temperature difference. Heat is not a property an object simply has while sitting still, it describes energy in the act of moving from one place to another; once the transfer stops, it no longer makes sense to call that energy heat, it has simply become part of the internal energy of whatever received it.

This distinction lines up with how each quantity is actually measured. Temperature is read off a scale, Celsius, Fahrenheit, or Kelvin, using a thermometer. Heat is measured in units of energy, such as joules or calories, and describes a quantity of energy transferred, not a reading on any instrument.

A useful way to see the difference clearly is to compare a lit match to a large tub of warm bathwater. The match flame can reach several hundred degrees Celsius, far hotter than bathwater sitting at around forty degrees Celsius. Yet because the tub contains vastly more total particles than the tiny flame, the bathwater actually holds, and could transfer, far more total thermal energy overall than the match does, despite its much lower temperature. Touch the match and it burns almost instantly, since a small amount of energy is delivered at extremely high temperature to a single small point of contact. Touch the bathwater and it merely feels pleasantly warm, since its far larger total energy is spread across a huge number of particles and transfers gradually, driven by a much smaller temperature difference from your skin. Temperature, an average per particle, and heat, or total thermal energy, which depends on both temperature and the total amount of substance present, are genuinely different quantities, and this example shows why conflating them leads to the wrong prediction.

Heat is just one particular way that energy moves from place to place, alongside work and, in nuclear contexts, other pathways. Temperature differences are what set the direction heat travels: heat always flows spontaneously from higher temperature toward lower temperature, continuing until both reach the same shared temperature, known as thermal equilibrium, and never spontaneously the other way. This is exactly why exothermic and endothermic reactions cause their surroundings to warm or cool at all: it is heat flowing down the temperature gradient that the reaction itself creates.
